exercises.title: Deep Dive: Designing and validating a SOC detection strategy from scratch
exercises.situation: A newly-formed SOC has a SIEM, an EDR, and cloud security tooling deployed, but almost no real detection coverage — mostly default, out-of-the-box rules. Leadership asks you to design and justify an actual detection strategy from the ground up, and to explain how you'd prove it's working, not just that it exists.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd turn on all the default detection rules that came with the tools and make sure alerts are going somewhere people can see them. That should give us good coverage.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: Relying entirely on default, out-of-the-box rules treats detection coverage as something a vendor ships rather than something built deliberately against this organization's own actual risks, and 'alerts are going somewhere people can see them' has no connection to whether those alerts would actually catch a real attack against this specific environment, or whether 'working' is ever actually measured.
exercises.professionalResponse: Default rules are a reasonable starting floor, but they're generic by design — they don't know what this organization's actual critical assets are, what a realistic attacker would actually target here, or what's already covered by another control. A real detection strategy has to be built deliberately, prioritized by actual risk, and then validated, not just switched on. I'd walk through how I'd build this from the ground up, and just as importantly, how I'd prove each piece is actually working rather than just enabled.

deepDive.heading: Starting from what actually matters to this organization, not a generic checklist
deepDive.content: Before writing a single detection rule, I'd identify this organization's actual crown-jewel assets and realistic threat scenarios — which systems hold the data or access that would cause the most damage if compromised, and which attack paths are realistically most likely given this organization's industry, exposure, and existing gaps. Generic, default rules treat every environment the same; a real strategy starts from what this specific SOC would actually need to catch to prevent its worst realistic day. I'd use a recognized framework — MITRE ATT&CK — to map likely attacker techniques against this organization's actual attack surface, rather than starting from whatever rules a vendor happened to ship by default.

deepDive.heading: Prioritizing detections by what's actually missing, not what's easiest to turn on
deepDive.content: I'd inventory what's already covered — by the EDR's own behavioral detections, by existing cloud security tooling, by any network-layer controls — before writing new SIEM correlation rules, specifically to avoid redundant detections that create alert noise without adding real coverage. I'd prioritize use-case development around the gaps: if the EDR already reliably catches a specific process-injection technique, a redundant SIEM rule for the same technique isn't a priority; if nothing currently detects lateral movement via a compromised service account, that's a real, prioritized gap to build a specific correlation rule for. Each new detection I build gets tied explicitly to a specific MITRE ATT&CK technique and a specific log source, so coverage can be tracked as a map, not a vague sense of 'we have some detections now.'

deepDive.heading: Building detections as testable hypotheses, not just rule logic
deepDive.content: Every detection I write, I'd frame as an explicit, testable claim: this rule should fire when X sequence of events happens within Y time window, and should not fire during normal legitimate activity of type Z. That framing is what makes the next step possible — I can't validate a detection I haven't stated precisely enough to test. I'd also deliberately tune each rule's time window and threshold based on this organization's actual log volume and behavior patterns, not a vendor's generic default, since a correlation rule's time window that's wrong for this environment's actual traffic volume will either miss real attacks or drown analysts in false positives.

deepDive.heading: Validating coverage with purple-team testing, not just trusting the rule logic
deepDive.content: Writing a detection rule that looks correct on paper isn't the same as confirming it actually fires against real attacker behavior in this specific environment. I'd validate the highest-priority detections through structured purple-team exercises: have a tester actually execute the specific technique the rule is meant to catch — the exact lateral movement technique, the exact credential-access pattern — in a controlled way, and confirm the rule fires, fires with enough fidelity to actually be actionable, and doesn't also fire constantly on unrelated legitimate activity. Any rule that fails this test — doesn't fire, fires too late, or fires on noise — gets tuned and retested before I'd ever claim it as real coverage, rather than leaving an unvalidated rule on the books that looks like coverage but isn't.

deepDive.heading: Proving the strategy is working on an ongoing basis, not as a one-time launch claim
deepDive.content: The final piece is making 'is this working' a continuously answerable question, not a one-time claim at launch. I'd track specific, concrete metrics over time: percentage of prioritized MITRE ATT&CK techniques with a validated, tested detection; mean time to detect and mean time to respond trends, specifically for incidents involving a technique we have a validated rule for, versus ones we don't; and the false-positive rate per rule, since a rule that's technically 'coverage' but gets tuned out or ignored by analysts within a month isn't actually providing the protection it looks like on paper. I'd report this to leadership not as 'detection strategy complete' but as a living map: here's our validated coverage percentage against the techniques that actually matter to us, here's what's still a known gap, and here's the plan to close it next, which is a fundamentally more honest and more useful claim than 'we turned on the default rules.'

vocabulary.term: Use-case development: building detections that matter
vocabulary.definition: The deliberate process of designing detection rules around an organization's specific, actual risks and gaps, rather than relying on generic, one-size-fits-all default rules.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the core discipline distinguishing a deliberately-built detection strategy from simply enabling whatever a vendor ships by default.
vocabulary.example: Use-case development meant prioritizing a rule for the specific lateral movement gap nothing currently covered, not just enabling every default rule available.

lessonLink.label: Use-Case Development: Building Detections That Matter

vocabulary.term: Hunting with MITRE ATT&CK as a map
vocabulary.definition: Using the MITRE ATT&CK framework's catalog of attacker techniques as a structured basis for both proactive threat hunting and systematic detection coverage planning.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the recognized framework that turns 'build good detections' into a trackable, specific map of covered versus uncovered attacker techniques.
vocabulary.example: I mapped our detection coverage directly against MITRE ATT&CK techniques, rather than describing coverage in vague terms.

lessonLink.label: Hunting with MITRE ATT&CK as a Map

vocabulary.definition: Designing a SIEM correlation rule's specific events, time window, and threshold deliberately for the organization's actual environment and behavior, rather than using a vendor's generic default configuration.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the concrete mechanism behind each prioritized detection, and tuning its time window and threshold to this organization's real traffic is what determines whether it actually works here.
vocabulary.example: I tuned the correlation rule's time window specifically to this organization's actual authentication traffic patterns, not a generic default.

lessonLink.label: Writing a Real-World Correlation Rule

vocabulary.term: Running a collaborative purple team exercise
vocabulary.definition: A structured exercise where an attacker-simulating tester and the defending team work together to execute specific attack techniques and directly validate whether detections actually fire as intended.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the specific validation method that proves a detection rule works against real attacker behavior, rather than just looking correct in its written logic.
vocabulary.example: The purple team exercise confirmed three of our new rules fired correctly, and revealed two that needed further tuning before they could be trusted.

lessonLink.label: Running a Collaborative Purple Team Exercise

vocabulary.term: Turning a purple team exercise into better detections
vocabulary.definition: Using the specific results of a purple-team validation exercise to directly tune and improve detection rules, closing the loop between testing and actual rule quality.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's what makes validation actually improve the strategy, rather than just confirming or disproving it without acting on the result.
vocabulary.example: The two rules that didn't fire cleanly during the exercise were tuned and retested until they met the same validation bar as the others.

lessonLink.label: Turning a Purple Team Exercise into Better Detections

vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's the general discipline this whole response is an application of — framing each rule as a testable hypothesis and tracking coverage as an ongoing, measurable map is the core of detection engineering as a field, beyond any single course's SIEM or SOC lesson.
